# How to succeed in this course {#how-to-succeed}

Success in QM is not about talent for mathematics. It is about a short
weekly routine that you repeat: **prepare before class, take part in class,
read and practise after class, and bring your attempts to the tutorial.**
Every lecture chapter is built around this routine. Every part of it has a
stated time budget, so you always know what "enough" looks like.

Why this routine works:

- If you prepare, the lecture is your second look at each idea, not your
  first. You can then use the lecture for questions and examples.
- The lecture covers the core of each chapter and leaves room for questions
  and for trying things out. The chapter has the full material, with every
  step, example, and piece of code. This is why the first step after class
  is to read the lecture material once in full.
- Answering a few recall questions on the same day stops you from
  forgetting, at the moment when that costs the least time.
- Each chapter has review questions on earlier lectures, because the exam
  covers the whole course.
- The tutorials prepare you for the exam only if you arrive with your own
  attempts. Wrong attempts are the most useful ones.

The total time outside class is about **4 hours per week** for QM Basic in
weeks with two lectures (about the same in tutorial weeks), and about
**1.5 to 2 hours per week** for QM Intermediate (2.5 hours in the two
tutorial weeks). Research on learning consistently finds that practice
spread over the weeks works better than the same hours packed together
before the exam.

## Minimum path and full path

Every chapter marks two paths through the work outside class.

- **Minimum path.** Before class: the video and the prediction (QM Basic) or
  the video and the R warm-up (QM Intermediate). After class: read the
  lecture material, answer the recall questions, then work for 10 minutes on
  the tasks that follow. This takes about 35 minutes after class. If a week
  is full, do this and nothing else. It keeps you in the course.
- **Full path.** All tasks in the chapter, with the stated time budgets. This
  is the preparation the exam assumes.

## What is examined

Each lecture has a **Must know** box. It separates what you must be able to
do yourself from what it is enough to recognise. **Definition** boxes belong
to the exam material. Grey **Optional** boxes do not: they hold formal
versions, derivations, and side topics for those who want them.

In class you will often be asked to try a question with your neighbour for
two or three minutes before the answer is shown. Take these minutes
seriously, even when the question looks hard. Most of the learning happens
there. In QM Intermediate, bring your laptop: the code shown in the lecture is
in the chapter, ready to copy, so you can run each step yourself and get the
same numbers and figures.

## Printable weekly checklists

Four week types cover the whole block. Print this page (the checklists print
cleanly without the site navigation) or copy the relevant list into your
planner at the start of each week.

### QM Basic: week with two lectures (weeks 43, 45, 47)

::: {.week-checklist}
#### Two-lecture week, about 4 hours outside class

- <span class="day">Friday before</span> (30 min, free morning): prep videos
  for Monday's lecture, prep task, prediction
- <span class="day">Monday</span>: 14:45 lecture · evening, 25 min: read the
  lecture material, answer the recall questions
- <span class="day">Tuesday</span> (60 min, free day): practice tasks for
  Monday's lecture · review questions from earlier lectures
- <span class="day">Wednesday</span> (30 min, around the single EiA slot):
  prep videos for Thursday's lecture, prep task, prediction
- <span class="day">Thursday</span>: 10:45 lecture · afternoon, 25 min: read
  the lecture material, answer the recall questions
- <span class="day">Friday</span> (60 min): practice tasks for Thursday's
  lecture · "Make it yours", two sentences · prepare for Monday
:::

### QM Basic: week with one lecture and a tutorial (weeks 44, 46, 48, 49)

::: {.week-checklist}
#### Lecture-plus-tutorial week

- <span class="day">Friday before</span> (30 min): prep for Monday's lecture
- <span class="day">Monday</span>: lecture (14:45, in week 44 at 10:45) · 25 min: read the lecture
  material, answer the recall questions
- <span class="day">Tuesday</span> (60 min): practice tasks for Monday's
  lecture
- <span class="day">Wednesday</span> (60 min): attempt the tutorial tasks
  yourself first, AI allowed under the protocol, mark stuck points
- <span class="day">Thursday</span>: tutorial at 10:45 or 12:45 (exam prep session),
  bring attempts · 15 min: redo the missed task
- <span class="day">Friday</span> (60 min): finish the tutorial set
  on your own · "Make it yours" · prepare for Monday
:::

### QM Intermediate: standard week (one Wednesday lecture)

The year 2 week is denser (two or three other lectures plus EiA3 and their
tutorials), so the QM work is one round per week, spread over several days.

::: {.week-checklist}
#### Standard week, 1.5 to 2 hours outside class

- <span class="day">Monday or Tuesday</span> (15--30 min, before the
  lecture): prep video, prep question, R warm-up, bring the output
- <span class="day">Wednesday</span>: QM lecture (the start time changes,
  see the table above), bring your laptop · evening, 25 min: read the lecture material,
  answer the recall questions
- <span class="day">Thursday or Friday</span> (50--60 min, around your EiA3
  slot): the practice tasks after class · one review question from an
  earlier lecture · "Make it yours", two sentences about your EiA3 venture
:::

### QM Intermediate: tutorial week (weeks 45 and 48)

The tutorial is the day after the lecture, so attempts cannot wait for the
end of the week. The tutorial covers the three preceding lectures. Each task
names the lecture it uses. Start with the tasks on the two earlier lectures.

::: {.week-checklist}
#### Tutorial week

- <span class="day">Monday or Tuesday</span> (75 min): prep for Wednesday's
  lecture (30) · attempt the tutorial tasks that rest on the earlier
  lectures (45), AI allowed under the protocol, mark stuck points
- <span class="day">Wednesday</span>: QM lecture · evening, 30 min: read the
  lecture material (15) · attempt the tutorial tasks that use today's
  lecture (15)
- <span class="day">Thursday</span>: tutorial (exam prep session), bring
  attempts and stuck points
- <span class="day">Friday</span> (45 min): redo what the tutorial
  corrected, on your own · "Make it yours"
:::

## Working with AI, in one paragraph

Use [Tilly](https://chatbot.tilburg.ai/) and other AI tools under the
standing protocol **Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain**. Attempt the task
yourself first and find where you are stuck. Ask for a hint or a diagnostic
question, not for a full solution. Verify every answer against the data, the
course notation, and the R output. Then explain the result in your own
words. The exam tests what you can do with supplied output. The protocol
makes AI sharpen that ability instead of replacing it.

## If you fall behind

Do not try to catch up by reading everything you missed. Go to the chapter of
the most recent lecture. Read its lecture material once, answer its recall
questions, and do its first practice task. Bring what you cannot solve to the
next tutorial or to Tilly. One finished round on the current lecture is worth
more than reading three older chapters without practising. The
[Mathematics Refresher](math-refresher.qmd) and
[R Refresher](r-refresher.qmd) are there so that a gap from an earlier course
never blocks this one.
